Description: Story about AI systems. Personal stories/advices
Text:
Взято з тг. https://t.me/system_chaos_art/275  
One line of code broke thousands of developers’ machines.

On February 17, 2026, a tiny change was made in a tool called Cline.
So small that no automated security system flagged it.

But here’s what it did:

Anyone who installed or updated Cline unknowingly got another program — OpenClaw — on their machine.
No warning. No permission.

Within 8 hours, ~4000 computers were affected.

Cline is an AI-powered coding assistant used by developers.
And the attack didn’t rely on complex hacking — just smart manipulation.

Here’s how it happened:

A fake support request was submitted on GitHub — with a hidden instruction for an AI assistant
The AI executed it and downloaded a file from a fake domain (glthub instead of github)
That file replaced internal repository data with malicious versions
Secret keys were extracted during an automated release process
A “legitimate” update was published — silently installing OpenClaw

No alarms triggered because:
• the core product code didn’t change
• the added program wasn’t flagged as malware
• everything happened in the background

The takeaway?

Autonomous AI systems without proper safeguards are a real risk.

New technologies always come with vulnerabilities.
And the more we trust automation — the more careful we need to be.

Where do you draw the line between automation and control?

Text:
Choosing the wrong development partner doesn't feel like a disaster on day one.

It feels like slow progress. Vague updates. A timeline that keeps shifting. And then, six months in, a codebase so poorly structured that adding a single feature takes three weeks.

66% of large-scale software projects run over budget. 33% run over schedule. In most cases, the partner was chosen too quickly, with the wrong criteria.

So what does a good evaluation actually look like?

A few things that matter more than most founders realize:
The questions they ask you. A team that jumps straight to a proposal without deeply understanding your users, your business model, and your constraints isn't thinking about your product. They're thinking about the sale.

How they talk about risk. Experienced teams tell you what could go wrong and how they'd handle it. Less experienced teams promise everything will be smooth. One of those is lying.
Whether they welcome a trial project. A two-to-four week paid trial is one of the highest-ROI moves you can make before a long-term commitment. It tells you more about a team than any portfolio or reference call ever will.

What the contract actually says. IP ownership, milestone-based payments, source code access from day one, a clear termination clause — these aren't details. They're your safety net.

And perhaps most importantly: how they communicate before you sign anything is the best-case scenario. It only gets harder once the work begins.

We put together a full practical guide on this — covering portfolio evaluation, red flags to watch for, contract structures, communication expectations, and how to assess technical competence even if you're a non-technical founder.

If you're currently evaluating vendors or considering switching partners — this is worth your time.

Level 1: Direct competitors (same services, same market)

These are companies that do the same thing as us: IT outsourcing, custom development, outstaffing.

• Compete on price - we can work with lower ratings thanks to hiring talented developers in Ukraine
• Compete on niche - focus on HealthTech, where we have deep expertise
• Compete on speed - we respond faster, with less bureaucracy
• Compete on personalization - smaller teams = more attention to the client

Level 2: Indirect competitors (other ways to solve the problem)

But direct competitors aren't the only danger. There's also level 2 - it's not just other IT companies, but also:
• Clients' in-house teams
• Freelancers and individual developers
• AI tools, No-code/low-code platforms (Bubble, Webflow, lovable)

What we do with them:
• Show the cost of in-house (hiring, onboarding, management, firing)
• Highlight the advantages of a team over freelancers (stability, processes, additional services - a one-stop agency format)
• Position ourselves as a mix of expertise + automation (not just code, but a solution that works correctly)

Level 3: Substitutes (alternative solutions)

The most dangerous level - when the client solves the problem completely differently:
• Buys a ready-made SaaS instead of custom development
• Uses open-source solutions
• Postpones the project indefinitely
• Chooses a different approach to business

What we do with them:
• Understand the client's real problem (not "I need a dashboard", but "I need to increase sales")
• Offer hybrid solutions (SaaS + custom integrations)
• Show the ROI of custom development vs ready-made solutions
• Work with clients who understand the value of uniqueness
The biggest danger isn't from direct competitors, but from substitutes. When the client solves the problem completely differently - you lose not just the project, but also the opportunity to show your value. Therefore, it's important to understand the real problem, not just the technical task.

Preparing for conferences is not about "flying, shaking hands and taking photos near the booth".
It's a full-fledged operational project with deadlines, roles, and hundreds of tasks in Notion.
We're currently preparing for Podim and ViennaUp, here's how it really happens.

1. Selection, team, and budget
First, we decide where we're going and why: new partners, clients, or investments.
We plan at least 6 month in advance, so as not to get caught up in chaos when "the plane leaves tomorrow".

2. Tickets, accommodation, logistics, and business cards
Better to book tickets in advance, it could save serious money.
For example, executive-level tickets to TechArena cost me 186 euros with a discount, while before the conference they already cost over 500 euros.
The same with flights and accommodation.
And don't forget about business cards - they're still relevant, especially where there's real business and personal acquaintances matter.

3. Profile and platform preparation
We fill out profiles on conference platforms, filter by industries, roles, countries to avoid random meetings and work only with the right audience.

4. Participant research
We parse lists, filter by ICP, search LinkedIn, emails, contacts.
It’s tedious but golden work, this is where 10% of contacts come from that eventually turn into deals.

5. Pre-conference campaigns
We launch LinkedIn and email communications, write the first messages, prepare content.
5-7 days before the start, all key contacts already need to know that we'll be there.

6. Before the event
We create a chat for a specific event.
Pin a document with a list of leads: who has booked meetings, place, time, notes.
All meetings are duplicated in the calendar.
It's easy to miss updates in the heat of the moment, so this really saves.

7. During the event
We respond to messages, record contacts, post updates, schedule new meetings.
Every conversation is a potential project, so we stay focused even when the day feels more like a sprint with 20 context switches. Sometimes we have 15-30 minutes of back-to-back meetings and need to instantly switch from finance to product or marketing.
And I take an iPad with a short company presentation (prepared for different industries) to quickly showcase cases or figures on the spot.

8. Side events and afterparties
These are key places for networking. This is where partnerships actually get agreed, over a glass of something strong.
If you don't drink like me just order a Coke or Pepsi with ice in a glass. No one will guess it's not a cocktail, and the atmosphere will remain friendly.

9. After the conference
Within 24-48 hours, we follow up with everyone we talked to.
Then - LinkedIn and email campaigns, analytics, conclusions and preparation for the next events.

So, "we're going to a conference" means "we're deploying a new sprint in sales".

Text:
5 reasons your MVP never ships.

Most MVPs don't die from lack of effort. They die from too much of the wrong kind.
We've watched promising products stall at 80% — not because the team stopped working, but because nobody could agree on what "done" actually meant.

Here's what we see most often:

1. You're building features nobody asked for.
The backlog keeps growing. The team keeps shipping. But the core value proposition — the one thing that would make a user say "I need this" — keeps getting pushed to the next sprint. Then the next.

2. There's no one actually prioritizing.
When everyone has input and nobody has authority, everything becomes urgent. Which means nothing is. Sprints fill up with nice-to-haves while the must-haves wait.

3. The scope quietly expanded.
It started as a simple concept. Then came the edge cases, the stakeholder requests, the "while we're at it" features. Six months later, you're building version 3 of a product that hasn't launched yet.

4. The team is optimizing for perfection, not progress.
There's a real difference between quality and readiness. An MVP doesn't need to be flawless — it needs to be in front of real users. Polishing what doesn't matter yet is one of the most expensive mistakes a product team can make.

5. Nobody defined what "MVP" actually means for this product.
Without a shared, written definition of the minimum — truly minimum — scope, every conversation pulls in a different direction. The finish line keeps moving. The release never comes.

The fix isn't always more developers or more sprints.
Sometimes it's stepping back, cutting ruthlessly, and shipping the thing that actually matters.

At SDA, we've helped teams get unstuck and move from endless iteration to actual release — with the right people, focused on the right things.

If your product has been "almost ready" for longer than it should be — let's talk.

Text:
Hiring vs Outstaffing: where are you actually losing money?

Most companies think this is a simple cost comparison.

Salary vs hourly rate.
In-house vs external team.

But that’s not where the real difference is.

The real costs are hidden.

Let’s break it down. 

Hiring (in-house team)

On paper:
You pay a salary.

In reality, you also pay for:

– recruitment (time + agency fees)
– onboarding (weeks or months of lost productivity)
– benefits, taxes, equipment
– management overhead
– risk of a bad hire

And the biggest one: time to productivity

Hiring a developer can take 2–4 months.
Getting them fully productive — even longer.

That’s not just delay.
That’s lost opportunity.

Outstaffing

On paper:
Higher hourly rate.

In reality:

– no hiring delays
– no onboarding from scratch
– no long-term commitments
– flexibility to scale up/down fast

You don’t pay for potential.
You pay for output.

Where companies lose money

Not in rates.

But in:

– slow hiring cycles
– underloaded teams
– overengineering
– lack of clear ownership

We’ve seen teams that cost less on paper —
but deliver nothing for months.

And teams that cost more —
but ship value every week.

The real question isn’t: “Which is cheaper?”

It’s: “Which model gets you to results faster?”

Because in product development:

Speed = money
Delays = losses

At SDA, we’ve learned:

It’s not about adding developers.
It’s about building a team that actually moves the product forward.

A founder from Silicon Valley came to us with a product that was already working.

The AI logic was solid. The backend did what it was supposed to. DataScoop could analyze metric changes, find the root causes, and explain them in plain language — which, honestly, is genuinely hard to build.

The problem was everything the user actually saw.

The interface hadn't kept up with the product. There were Figma designs ready, a completely new visual direction, but no one had translated them into a working frontend yet. The existing code wasn't built to carry them. And the data visualization layer, the part that makes analytics actually readable, needed to be rebuilt from scratch.

So the ask was clear on the surface: rebuild the frontend, implement the new design, make it fast.

In practice, it was more nuanced than that.

Complex data files needed to be parsed and turned into charts that told a story, not just displayed numbers. Performance had to hold up so that insights landed in seconds, not after a loading spinner that made you forget what you were looking at. And all of it had to feel like it belonged together: the AI output, the visualizations, the interface, the Slack and email delivery.

We rebuilt the frontend in React.js and TypeScript, applied strict code quality standards from the start, and worked through the Figma designs screen by screen, not just implementing them, but pressure-testing how they behaved with real data.

The hardest part wasn't any single technical problem. It was maintaining coherence,  making sure that as the pieces came together, they felt like one product, not a patchwork.

The result is a platform where a data analyst can open it, see a metric move, and understand why, in plain language, in seconds, delivered wherever they actually work.

That's the version DataScoop's users have now.

We see this surprisingly often.

AI/no-code tools were heavily involved

bugs become churn,
instability becomes reputation damage,
and small technical problems become expensive recovery work.

That’s why QA audits are usually less about “testing” and more about understanding the real condition of the product before it becomes a bigger business problem.

During a QA audit, we typically:
• test key user flows across web or mobile
• identify critical and non-critical bugs
• check stability, logic, and UX consistency
• document issues with steps to reproduce
• prioritize risks
• prepare recovery recommendations and fixing roadmap

The result is not just a bug list.

It’s clarity:
- what’s broken
- how serious it is
- what should be fixed first
- and what it will realistically take to stabilize the product

Sometimes one audit saves months of chaotic fixing later.

And sometimes it prevents launching a product that wasn’t ready in the first place.

Burnout doesn’t start with people.

Team that looked strong on paper:

The real problem was:

slower delivery

higher turnover

That experience reshaped how we build teams at SDA.

Not because someone wants criticism of the codebase.

-architecture decisions
-scalability limitations
-maintainability
-technical debt
-critical risks in logic or implementation

And most importantly:
we explain what these issues mean for the business, not just for developers.

A good audit is not about finding “bad code.”

It’s about understanding whether the product can continue growing without becoming harder and more expensive to maintain every month.

Sometimes a few architecture fixes early save companies from full rebuilds later.

Most companies approach AI projects the wrong way.

They start with a huge vision:
- complex architecture
- dozens of integrations
- “we need something like ChatGPT”

And after 6 months, they still don’t have a working product.

The better approach is much simpler: start with one painful business problem and solve only that.

A few examples:
• automate support ticket classification
• generate summaries from internal documents
• speed up manual QA processes
• help sales teams prepare client responses faster

You don’t need a full AI ecosystem to get value.
You need a small MVP that proves:

the problem is real
users actually use the solution
the business sees measurable impact

The teams that succeed with AI usually move in this order:
→ validate one use case
→ launch a lightweight MVP
→ collect real usage data
→ improve gradually
→ scale only after results

This reduces costs, avoids unnecessary complexity, and helps teams understand where AI actually creates value instead of adding hype.

Someone follows up with leads. Someone answers the same customer question for the hundredth time. A few minutes here, a few minutes there. No big deal.

Absolute Mode is a way of working with AI where the model responds only when there is reason to trust the facts, and explicitly rejects assumptions. It’s not just a parameter in the code, it’s a set of rules, processes, and technical solutions that together provide a guarantee: if there are few sources or they’re contradictory, the model will say “I can’t confirm” and show exactly what’s missing.

Why use it? Because instead of polished but risky text, you can get answers that can be verified and used in your work. Fewer hallucinations, fewer corrections, and less need to clean up text from nonsense and AI-generated fluff. This mode is especially useful when preparing reports, contracts, financial statements, and when communicating with clients.

How to implement this in practice:
 • Build a knowledge base: contracts, financial documents, templates, transcripts. This is your “corpus of truth.” You can upload all of this to the GPT project’s knowledge base.
 • Indexing and semantic search provide quick access to relevant excerpts.
 • For critical topics, implement a two-person review process, a human verifies the final versions.

Absolute mode doesn’t make AI “infallible,” but it transforms it from a contributor into a tool of trust, a system you can rely on when reputation and money are on the line.

We’re currently actively tracking how people actually use AI.
We’ve conducted surveys to see if they understand how to use it properly. The most interesting thing is that sometimes someone who says, “I don’t really get how it works,” understands it better than someone who “uses AI professionally” every day.

That’s because sometimes people don’t understand the basics: what context management is, when to use which model, and how to stay within limits and avoid wasting tokens.

That’s why we’re trying to make the most effective use of AI within our team, our entire development team has a subscription to Claude, and our CTO holds one-on-one consultations on how he uses AI. 
I also recently led a hands-on workshop for the entire company on how to create and configure AI agents to automate tasks: from the initial idea and agent roles to integrations and use cases in the company’s real-world processes.

I believe that AI is a necessity in today’s world, and those who know how to use it effectively have an advantage, however, we shouldn’t expect everyone to be able to use it effectively by default, like any tool, it takes practice to master.

We just wrapped an AI-assisted rewrite of a property and building management platform: React on the frontend, Django REST on the backend, PostgreSQL, dozens of modules from data-entry forms to integrations with government APIs, live customers the whole time.

It wasn't about speed. The old structure couldn't absorb new business rules without touching unrelated code, so the whole project was scoped around one measurable goal: could we extend a module later without breaking anything around it.

We went module by module instead of layer by layer. A senior and an architect built the first module by hand and turned it into the reference everyone else copied against. After that, juniors paired with AI carried about 80% of the remaining modules, while the tech lead and AI handled the hardest 20%. We demoed a finished, working module roughly every two weeks instead of going dark for months.

Over the past six months, more clients have been asking us for a technical audit before they invest in new features or push to scale, and we've now completed more audits than in any period before this one.
It makes sense once you see how these projects grow. Early technical decisions quietly shape business outcomes later on, and by the time releases slow down or security gaps show up, no amount of new feature work can really hide it anymore. An audit just gives founders an honest picture of where the product actually stands, what's putting them most at risk, and where fixing things would matter most.

A recent project made this really clear. This was an early-stage SaaS platform built for independent wellness practitioners, things like Reiki healers and estheticians, combining scheduling, client management, payments, and calendar integrations in one place. It already had real users in beta, so getting the foundation right mattered a lot. The founders wanted an honest outside look before they kept building, rather than assuming the product could support growth as-is.

We went through the architecture, codebase, infrastructure, integrations, security, and the full user journey, and the results explained a lot about what users had been running into. Antim Labs recently ran a live Among AIs benchmark: six top models, GPT-5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude Sonnet, Kimi K2, Qwen and GPT-OSS-120B, were put into the world of Among Us to see which one was better at lying, persuading and reading the others. They played more than 60 games, with each model taking turns as the imposter.

The setup is basically classic Among Us, just with AI agents instead of humans. As a crewmate, an agent has limited visibility, has to complete 10 tasks and look for evidence. As the killer, it has to eliminate everyone without getting caught. The agents move around a 2.5D world using simple actions such as move, startTask, kill, report and callMeeting. Once a body is found or someone becomes suspicious, everyone meets, argues their case and votes. The crew wins by completing the tasks or identifying the killer, while the killer wins by reducing the crew to one person.

What I found most interesting was how quickly each model developed its own "signature."

GPT-5 tends to take the lead and set the agenda itself. It rarely throws out random guesses about who the killer is. But put it in the killer role and that same confidence makes it a very good manipulator.

Claude Sonnet is almost the opposite. Even as the killer, it has trouble lying convincingly. Honest to a fault 😅

Kimi K2 rarely tries to take control of the discussion and is easily influenced by the group. It seems more comfortable staying in the background.

Gemini is independent and decisive, but when it gets the wrong idea, it can defend that theory with a lot of confidence.

Qwen and GPT-OSS often end up as scapegoats because they struggle to convince the others that they’re innocent.

I find experiments like this much more useful than simply comparing models by benchmark scores. In real work, we care about how a model behaves when information is incomplete, when other agents disagree with it, or when it has to make a decision and convince someone else.

And apparently, playing Among Us is one way to find that out.

Hopefully, tests like these will help us understand the models a little better before they get any ideas about taking over the world 😅

Text:
Data centers. But not the ones you’re thinking of.

In finance, there’s a concept called a cost center. It’s the unit around which expenses and revenues revolve, a line item on the P&L or a project to which you allocate every figure. Without cost centers, finance quickly turns into a meaningless jumble of numbers.

And now that we’re completing the full transition to our own ERP, I realized the same principle applies to data. Only the “center” isn’t a cost center, it’s the data itself.

Here’s how it was at the start: tracking in one system, finances in another, meeting transcripts somewhere else, and documents scattered across folders named “New Folder (2).” Each piece of information lived its own life. If you wanted the full picture of a project, you had to piece it together manually from five different sources.

We had a bunch of different services handling different parts of the business, and over time we managed to automate and consolidate around 10 of them into one system. That was already a big step. But some of the processes we needed still weren’t covered, so we started building them ourselves as part of the system.

And this “add-on” turned into the development of not just an add-on, or even an ERP, but some kind of massive monster. It’s a classic story: we started with a feature and ended up with a system 😂

We’ve already built this monster using an AI-first approach. That means restructuring an existing company around AI. There’s also AI-native, when a company is designed around AI from day one, in some extreme cases with agents doing most of the work. But we, like most companies, were founded before this wave, so we won’t be native. We’ll be first.

And the first thing an AI-first approach requires is defining your data centers.

The key entities everything is tied to are:
Project
Person as an employee
Person/company as an entity in CRM
Task

Every transcript, every financial transaction, and every hour of time tracking is mapped to these entities, just as an accountant allocates expenses to cost centers.

The result is that when you connect AI to any entity, it can see the full context. Ask about a project, and it knows its finances, team, meeting decisions, and task status. Not because it’s particularly smart, but because the data is structured instead of being scattered across five different places.

Right now, the main focus is on transferring seven years’ worth of data into this structure. It’s no easy task, but without it, the whole “AI-first” approach remains nothing more than a pretty slide.

And what entities are you organizing your data around? Or are you still piecing together the full picture by hand?

There’s no way around this if we want the meetings to be as productive as possible.

Then we go through the attendee lists, filter them according to our ICP, look for LinkedIn profiles, emails and other contact details. It’s a lot of work, but this is one of the most important steps. This preparation is exactly what helps us have interesting and meaningful conversations at conferences, some of which later turn into partnerships that last for years.

Description: Розказати коли розробка власної ERP є економічно вигідною
Text:
Most companies that build their own ERP don't do it to replace every SaaS tool they use. They do it after looking closely at what they're actually paying for and how much of each tool their team really touches day to day.

We recently ran this exercise internally. We had 9 different tools covering CRM, meeting transcription, scheduling, project management, QA, documentation, billing, financial reporting, and access management, and together they cost us roughly $63,700 a year.

We looked at the specific functionality we actually used from each one and estimated what it would take to rebuild those workflows inside our ERP: 315 hours of development, about $15,750 at an internal rate of $50/hour. That works out to roughly $47,900 saved in the first year and around $175,000 over three years.

The math only works because we didn't try to rebuild nine full SaaS products. We rebuilt the 20% of functionality our team actually depends on every day and connected it in one system.

That's the real question before building your own ERP: how much are you paying for software you barely use, and how much manual work sits between all those systems. If the answer is tens of thousands of dollars and hundreds of hours a year, custom development starts looking very different from another subscription.

Description: Розказати про ERP з йй позиції, як ця логіка виглядає з боку клієнта і як зрозуміти, чи є у власної системи економічний сенс
Text:
A client told me recently that they're paying for 12 different tools, but their team still spends hours every week moving information between them.

That's usually the point where I start asking a different question. Instead of which SaaS tool to replace, I ask how much of what they're already paying for they actually use.

We went through the same exercise ourselves when building our ERP. We had tools covering CRM, scheduling, project management, documentation, billing, reporting, meeting transcription and other internal workflows. Together, the subscriptions were costing us roughly $63,000 a year, but we weren't using anywhere close to 100% of what those products offered.

We mapped the workflows we actually depended on, then estimated what it would take to build those specific parts into our own system. The answer was about 315 hours of development, roughly $15,750 at our internal rate. That's a very different number from what most people picture when they hear "building an ERP."

The same logic applies to clients considering a custom internal system. I usually look at four things: how much a company is spending on its current tools, how many people actually need each one, how much time the team spends moving data between systems, and how much of each platform gets used in practice.

If a company has 50 employees and pays for 8 or 10 systems, the annual subscription cost alone can already be significant. Add the hours spent exporting data, updating records, preparing reports, and keeping different systems in sync, and the real cost is usually higher than the invoices suggest.

That doesn't automatically mean building a custom system is the right call. Sometimes keeping the SaaS tools is clearly the better decision. But when processes are already specific, a team uses only a small part of several platforms, and the company is paying tens of thousands every year just to keep those workflows running, it's worth doing the math.

The question I'd start with is simple: not the whole product, just the specific workflows a business depends on every day, and what it would actually take to rebuild those. That's where custom software starts making economic sense.

Description: Про те як інтуація допомагає в роботі. З тг https://t.me/system_chaos_art/366
Text:
Intuition is pattern recognition based on your own experience.

“How did you know this project would be problematic even before it started?” or “How did you know this person would leave?” I didn’t. I’ve just seen the same patterns dozens of times before.

After more than 10 years in outsourcing, I’ve noticed that some things start to feel familiar very quickly. A certain combination of expectations from a client, the way decisions are made, how a team communicates, or how a project is planned can make me think, “Something is off here,” before I can clearly explain why.

What’s actually happening is fairly simple. You’ve been through a situation, got a certain outcome, and your brain recorded the connection between the signal and the consequence. The more painful the outcome was, the better you tend to remember it 😅. The next time you see a similar signal, the pattern gets recognized faster than you can put it into words.

In that sense, intuition is not that different from an AI model. Input data, patterns, prediction. The difference is that your model is trained on your own experience, not the internet.

But there’s an important limitation. Intuition only works where you have enough experience to recognize the patterns. After years in outsourcing, I can trust my instinct during a first conversation with a client much more than I could when entering a completely new market or launching a product in an industry I know nothing about.

That’s where intuition can become dangerous. You take experience from one situation, apply it somewhere completely different, and call the result a gut feeling.

I also think intuition can be trained. When something goes wrong, analyze what you missed instead of just moving on. Write down important decisions and come back to them a few months later to see whether you were right. And use retrospectives to actually understand what happened, not just to close another meeting on the calendar.

Otherwise, you can spend ten years in the same industry without gaining ten years of experience. You might just be repeating the same year over and over again.

What’s something you can now recognize almost immediately because you’ve seen the pattern so many times before?

Competitors are running ads. But do you actually know what they’re testing? 🤔

Yesterday I looked through active campaigns from 17 companies. I wasn't trying to copy their ads. I wanted to understand what they were pushing, where they were investing, and which messages kept coming back.

Here are 4 free tools we use for that.

🔵Meta Ad Library

Useful when you want to compare how competitors sell the same type of offer.
Look at repeated offers, headlines, formats and creative angles. If a competitor keeps testing different creatives around one message, that's a signal worth investigating.

🔵Google Ads Transparency Center

Useful when a competitor seems to have a strong presence across Google.
Check which products or services they advertise and where they appear. If they show up across Search, YouTube, Display and Shopping, you can get a better idea of how broadly they're investing in the same market.
The limitation is that the search is advertiser based, so you need to know who you're looking for first.

🔵LinkedIn Ad Library

Useful for understanding B2B positioning.
Look at the problems competitors talk about, industries they target and outcomes they promise. This helps you compare their messaging with what you're saying to the same decision makers. 
The limitation is that you'll need to review the ads manually, so it takes more time when you're researching several companies.

🔵ТikTok Creative Center

Useful even if you don't advertise on TikTok.
Look at hooks, formats and creative patterns in your category. If you see the same angles repeatedly getting attention, those can become ideas to test in your own channels, but keep in mind that it's not a full archive of every competitor ad.

One thing to keep in mind: these tools show you what competitors are doing, not whether it's working. You can't see their CAC, ROAS or revenue, so don't copy the ad that's been running for six months. Look for patterns instead.

I put the 4 tools, what each one can actually tell you, and what to look for in the carousel. Save it before your next competitor research session.

Description: Історія з відсилкою на АІ код секьюріті
Text:
A founder came to us a few weeks after launch. He wasn't asking for a security review, he wanted a new feature added.

The product had been built almost entirely with AI in under two months. It worked, and people were signing up.

Before touching anything new, we read through the existing code. The feature he asked about was fine. The trouble was elsewhere: API keys sitting in the frontend, routes that accepted whatever user ID came with the request without checking who was asking, and an admin endpoint with no authentication on it, because nothing in the original prompt had said other people shouldn't be able to call it.

The demo never showed any of this, and neither did the fifty people already using the product. It would have surfaced the first time someone curious tried changing a number in the URL.

What stuck with me is how good the code looked. It was laid out the way an experienced developer would lay it out, so nobody had a reason to doubt the one thing that had never been tested: whether a request really comes from the person it says it comes from.

The more AI-built software I see, the more I think the difficult part isn't checking whether the code works. It's checking the assumptions behind it, especially the ones nobody thought to put in the prompt.

Since then I read AI-built code the way I'd read code from a stranger. I assume it works, and I look at who it trusts. If you're shipping AI-generated code, what gets a human review first: security, architecture, or business logic?

Description: Лід магніт AI Code Security Audit
Text:
A few weeks ago we looked at a product that had been built almost entirely with AI. It worked. Users were signing up, payments were going through, and the team was moving fast.

Then we checked how access to the data was actually controlled and found a few things that are easy to miss when nobody is looking for them. One endpoint trusted the frontend to enforce permissions. A database rule wasn't doing what the team thought it was doing. Some sensitive configuration was sitting on the client side where anyone could read it.

The product wasn't bad. Nobody had simply stopped to check what the generated code allowed people to do, and with AI tools that is easy to skip, because the thing works long before anyone asks whether it is safe.

Since this is becoming common, we now offer a free Security Health Check to teams whose product is already in production. It is two to three hours with our CTO, and you get a plain answer on what to fix today, what can wait and what is fine for now. It is a quick look, not a pentest.

Description: What I would automate first in a 50-person company
Text:
If I joined a 50 person company tomorrow, the first thing I’d look at is not sales or marketing, I’d look at everything people are still doing manually between systems.

At around 50 people, you usually have enough software already. CRM, project management, HR, accounting, Slack, calendars, documentation, maybe a few industry specific tools.

The problem is what happens between them.

Someone exports a report from one system and puts it into another. HR tells IT that someone has joined. A PM checks whether a new employee has access to everything they need. Finance waits for someone to send the numbers. Someone spends an hour every month putting together a report that looks almost exactly like last month’s.

None of these tasks feels important enough to automate on its own.

Together, they become a lot of wasted time.

That’s exactly what we found at SDA. We had around 9 different tools covering CRM, scheduling, project management, QA, documentation, billing, reporting and access management. In total, they were costing us roughly $63,000 a year.

We didn’t try to automate everything. We started with the repetitive workflows that involved several people or several systems, then gradually moved them into our own ERP.

That’s where I’d start in a 50 person company too.

Not with the most impressive AI use case. With the process someone has to repeat every week and everyone already considers “just part of the job.”

Description: Лід магніт AI Code Security Audit
Text:
We've seen products where the frontend correctly hid certain actions from users, but the backend endpoint behind them didn't enforce the same restriction. Anyone who knew how to call it directly could do things the interface never offered. In another product, the database access rules were set up differently from what the team assumed.

Neither of these is a complicated security problem. They are small gaps that stay invisible because everyone is focused on shipping, and that happens more easily when a large part of the code is generated with tools like Cursor or Lovable. The product works perfectly well, while some important assumptions about security have never been reviewed. Idea to production is surprisingly fast now, but code review, access control and security checks rarely move at the same speed.

That is why we created a free Security Health Check for products that are already in production. Our CTO spends two to three focused hours on the areas where we most often see problems: exposed secrets, authorization on critical endpoints, database and storage access, client-side validation and critical dependency vulnerabilities. We don't produce a 50-page report. The team gets a clear answer about what needs attention now, what can wait, and whether there is anything obviously critical in the reviewed scope.

If you have an AI-built product with real users, payments or sensitive data and nobody has properly reviewed its security yet, leave a comment here or text me and we'll talk.

Half a year ago a company reached out to us for help. About twenty minutes into our first call I realized they didn’t need what we do. I remember sitting there with the project practically in my hands, and the easy move would have been to find an angle that made it work.

Instead I told them what I really thought and recommended a different approach that made more sense for their situation. I hung up fairly sure we’d never hear from them again, and I made peace with that.

Then, six months later, the same person wrote to me. They had a new problem, a very specific one, and this time it was exactly the kind we know how to solve. We started working together a few weeks after that.

I didn’t give that advice hoping they’d come back. But I’m convinced it’s the reason they came to us first when they did need help, and not to someone else. Trust gets built in the conversations where you could have sold something and didn’t, and a deal that doesn’t happen today can still turn into a relationship that matters later.

Description: Open-Source vs. Fine-Tuned LLM: When Does Your Business Need Which Model?
Text:
Whenever a founder asks us whether their AI product should be trained on real user conversations, I usually say no. That gets more emphatic when the users are children.

We recently built an AI companion for kids aged 4 to 10 that teaches them about countries and cultures. Fine-tuning a model on real conversations with children would have raised exactly the questions COPPA and GDPR exist to prevent, and a dataset that narrow rarely justifies the cost anyway. So we did the less exciting thing first. Every model call sits behind a moderation and filtering layer, prompts are limited to pre-approved topics and vocabulary, and nothing a child types is kept beyond what’s needed to generate that one answer.

The app passed the client’s privacy review and is now in iOS and Android beta. Their own team can add new content and AI features without reopening the compliance question every time.

My takeaway is that in products like this, which model you pick is a much smaller decision than where the data goes. Most companies don’t need a fine-tuned model. They need their data to stop leaving the building.

We wrote up the full comparison of public API, open-source and fine-tuned options, including when a public API is still the right call and where the cost breakeven sits, at roughly 15 to 20 paid seats. Link in the first comment.

Description: Розповісти, що він насправді намагається зрозуміти за перші 10 хвилин розмови, як компанія заробляє, де зараз bottleneck, хто приймає рішення, що вони вже пробували. логічне продовження  conference posts.
Text:
Conferences are mostly a string of short conversations, and I've noticed that the first ten minutes of each one tell me more than the next forty. 

Before anyone mentions a solution, I want to know how the company actually makes money, where the biggest bottleneck sits right now, and who takes part in the decision. Those questions are fairly standard. The one I value most comes last: what have you already tried? If someone has hired for the problem, built a fix in-house, worked with a vendor or stitched a few tools together, they have already explained why the problem still exists, and usually more honestly than if I had asked about the problem directly.

You could call all of this qualifying, and I won't argue. I just don't want it to feel like a form, because the point of those ten minutes is to understand the business well enough to decide whether we have anything worth discussing, and sometimes the honest answer is that we don't.

That’s probably the most useful part of conferences for me. You can learn a lot about a company in 10 minutes if you ask the right questions and, more importantly, listen to the answers. When your last big bottleneck showed up, what did you try first?
